## 7. Workstream plans

### 7.1 Collection A — Parish registers

**Conservation.** The conservator works from 5 January to 13 February on the 220 volumes with binding failure: 30 working days at about 7–8 volumes/day. Each volume gets a condition record and a stabilisation treatment appropriate to a brittle binding. Volumes are scanned only after the conservator releases them. The book cradle is used for every volume; spines are never pressed. The 1,580 stable volumes are scanned first so that conservation is not on the critical path for the whole collection.

**Scanning.** Bindwell is on site at CRO from 2 February. The plan uses 24 scanning days at 75 volumes/day, finishing on 5 March. The stable volumes are scanned from 2 February; the 220 stabilised volumes join from 16 February. If throughput falls to 60 volumes/day, scanning takes 30 days and finishes on 13 March; the additional six days cost £4,200 and are covered by contingency (see section 8.4). CRO's two existing copystands are the fallback for additional capacity, using existing staff; they are not in the base budget.

**Image and QC.** Masters are captured at 400 ppi, 24-bit colour, with a colour target and resolution test at the start of each session. Every file gets an automated technical check (resolution, colour, skew, cropping, file integrity) and a 10% visual sample. Exceptions are re-scanned within the Bindwell booking. Checksums are recorded at capture and re-verified at ingest. Condition checks are logged before and after scanning.

**Publication.** Collection A is public domain, so publication is unrestricted. Catalogue records, IIIF manifests and access derivatives are built in April–May. The collection goes live on 10 June, three weeks before the grant deadline.

### 7.2 Collection B — Wrenfield Film Society

**Rights.** The Rights & Permissions Officer completes a documented risk assessment for each of the 240 reels in 15 working days (5–23 January), about 26 minutes per reel on average. The assessment records the reel identity, provenance, rightsholder search, orphan-work status, risk rating and publication decision. The Partnership's solicitor reviews the method and a sample of records; the Director signs off the assessment on 27 January. No B file is published before that sign-off. Publication carries a clear rights statement and a takedown policy. If a reel is assessed as high-risk, the Partnership escalates it to the funder rather than quietly dropping it; the plan assumes all 240 can be published with documented risk acceptance.

**Storage and handling.** All 240 reels remain in the Northgate cold store at 4°C and 35% RH when not being scanned. They move through the pass-through hatch into the inspection room at 16°C and 45% RH. The conservation policy's limits are applied as hard limits: no more than 40 reels out of the cold store at once, and no more than 30 minutes out of the cold store including scanning. The planning batch is 4 reels at 6 minutes/reel: 24 minutes of scanning plus 6 minutes of transfer and logging. Six batches per day give 24 reels/day; ten days give 240 reels. The first morning is a calibration trial; if the cycle is slower, the batch size is reduced (2 reels at 10 minutes/reel, or 1 reel at 15 minutes/reel) and the booking is extended only within the contingency and with the conservator's approval. The 30-minute rule is never relaxed.

**Scanning.** Filmtek is delivered and installed on 13 February and scans from 16 to 27 February. The scanner is never operated in the cold store. A calibrated temperature/RH logger runs throughout; if conditions leave 15–20°C or 40–50% RH, scanning stops. Each evening, files are copied to an encrypted drive and carried to CRO; the drive is logged, virus-checked, checksum-verified and ingested. No B files are left only at Northgate.

**QC and publication.** B QC and metadata run from 2 to 20 March. Every reel is checked for image integrity, frame count, colour, stability and file naming; the rights record is linked to the catalogue record. B publishes on 15 April, leaving ten weeks before the grant deadline.

### 7.3 Collection C — Harrow Estate papers

C is outside the base plan. The 950 boxes are subject to a donor restriction to 2030; the estate's written permission is required before any publication. The solicitor's August 2025 advice is that a decision is unlikely before autumn 2026; the September 2025 verbal assurance is not sufficient. In addition, 76 boxes (8%) are mould-affected and need isolation and treatment before scanning.

The only C actions in 2026 are:

- a written permission request on 19 January;
- a decision gate on 31 March;
- a record of the outcome.

No grant spend is committed. If written permission arrives, any C work is a separate costed variation. It cannot be funded by diverting A or B resources without putting the two-collection condition at risk. The recommendation is a 2026–27 proposal with its own mould treatment and digitisation budget.

### 7.4 Digital preservation and publication

- **Masters:** uncompressed TIFF for A; preservation-quality film scans for B, with the captured format agreed with Filmtek before booking.
- **Access:** JPEG derivatives for A; H.264/MP4 access copies for B, with captions/transcripts where the content warrants them.
- **Storage:** preservation masters and access copies in the Partnership's storage, with a 3-2-1 backup pattern (primary, on-site copy, off-site copy). Storage is budgeted at £250/month for six months.
- **Integrity:** SHA-256 checksums at capture, on transfer and at ingest; a fixity check before publication and at close.
- **Catalogue:** item-level records for A and reel-level records for B, with persistent identifiers and IIIF manifests.
- **Publication:** collection landing pages, search and browse, rights statements, takedown policy, accessibility audit and user testing.
- **Accessibility:** the audit covers keyboard navigation, alt text, colour contrast, captions/transcripts and document accessibility. Remediation is budgeted at £600.

### 8.4 Contingency release rules

The £5,220 contingency is not a general overspend fund. It is released by the Programme Manager with the Partnership Director's approval, against a written change note, in this order of priority:

1. **Filmtek throughput remediation — up to £3,500.** If the day-one calibration shows the 240-reel target cannot be met in ten days, extend the booking by up to three days (£3,600) or adjust the batch protocol. The 30-minute conservation limit is never relaxed.
2. **Bindwell throughput remediation — up to £3,500.** If A scanning runs at 60 volumes/day instead of 75, six extra days cost £4,200; the first £3,500 comes from contingency and the balance from virement against metadata or publication lines, with Director approval.
3. **Re-scans, replacement drives and minor price increases — up to £1,720.** Only with a receipted change note.

If both major throughput risks occur, the contingency cannot cover both. The Programme Manager must escalate to the Director and the funder with a revised scope or a variation request. The plan does not assume a further injection of funds.

### 8.5 What is not funded

- **Collection C:** no grant spend; no mould treatment, scanning or publication.
- **Equipment purchase:** the plan hires scanners; it does not buy them.
- **VAT:** assumed recoverable; if irrecoverable, the plan needs a 20% scope reduction or a funder discussion.
- **Permanent staff:** all staff costs are time-limited programme days, not permanent posts.
- **Partnership in-kind:** CRO and Northgate facilities, utilities, insurance, solicitor review, donor liaison time and communications are provided in-kind and are not charged to the grant.

## 9. Rationale for the major choices

### 9.1 Why two collections, not three

The grant requires at least two collections fully digitised and published. Collection C cannot lawfully be published without the Harrow estate's written permission, which the estate's own solicitor says is unlikely before autumn 2026. A verbal assurance is not a permission. Trying to include C would either breach the donor restriction or divert resources from A and B and risk the two-collection condition. The maximum compliant scope is therefore A and B in full, with C deferred. This is not a reduction in ambition; it is the largest publishable scope the rights position allows.

### 9.2 Why A and B are sequenced in parallel, not one after the other

A and B use different sites, different equipment and different specialist skills. A needs the CRO book cradle and the conservator; B needs the Northgate cold store and the Filmtek. Running them in parallel uses the February window efficiently and leaves April–June for quality control and publication. A strictly sequential plan (A then B) would push B scanning into April or May and leave no buffer before 30 June.

### 9.3 Why nitrate is scanned at Northgate, not CRO

CRO is not certified for film. The 2024 pilot failed at CRO when humidity reached 62%, condensation appeared on 14 frames, and the conservator stopped the run. The Northgate inspection room is 16°C and 45% RH, inside Filmtek's 15–20°C and 40–50% RH range, and it is adjacent to the licensed cold store with a pass-through hatch. Northgate is the only compliant location. The absence of a network is managed with encrypted drives and chain-of-custody, not by moving nitrate to CRO.

### 9.4 Why the Filmtek booking is exactly two weeks

Filmtek requires a two-week booking; ten working days is the minimum purchase. At the planning rate of 24 reels/day, ten days cover 240 reels with time each day for QC, re-scans and cold-store returns. A longer booking would add £1,200/day and is not needed on the planning assumptions. The day-one calibration is the control: if the cycle is slower, the batch size falls and the booking is extended only if the contingency can cover it.

### 9.5 Why 220 volumes are stabilised before scanning

About 12% of the 1,800 volumes (216, rounded to the conservator's 220) have binding failure. Scanning them on a book cradle without stabilisation would risk further damage. The conservator's six-week estimate (30 working days) is scheduled from 5 January to 13 February. The 1,580 stable volumes are scanned from 2 February, so conservation does not delay the start of A scanning. The brittle volumes join from 16 February and are finished within the Bindwell window.

### 9.6 Why the B rights assessment is done in January

The assessment is the longest lead-time rights task: 240 per-reel records, about three weeks of staff time. Doing it in January means it is signed off before any B scanning or publication, and any high-risk reel is identified while there is still time to adjust the publication plan. Leaving it until after scanning would put the publication date and the grant condition at risk. The assessment is reviewed by the solicitor and signed off by the Director; it is not a desk exercise completed after the fact.

### 9.7 Why publication is phased — B in April, A in June

B is smaller (240 reels) and its rights position is resolved in January, so it can be published first. Publishing B in April proves the publication pipeline, gives the team a real accessibility and user-testing cycle, and leaves A's larger metadata and QC workload a clear run to June. A publishes on 10 June, three weeks before the deadline. The phasing creates two independent chances to meet the grant condition, rather than one all-or-nothing June launch.

### 9.8 Why Bindwell rather than MobileScan for A

Bindwell is a book-cradle scanner at £700/day, designed for bound volumes and available at CRO from 1 February. MobileScan is £950/day plus £1.50 per item and handles paper only; for 1,800 bound volumes it would be more expensive and less suitable for brittle bindings. MobileScan is not nitrate-capable, so it is not an alternative for B. The CRO's two copystands are kept as fallback capacity for A, not as the primary solution.

### 9.9 Why the budget has a 6.2% contingency

The two throughput assumptions — 75 volumes/day on Bindwell and 24 reels/day on Filmtek — are planning assumptions, not contractual guarantees. A 6.2% contingency covers a modest overrun on either, not both. It is deliberately not larger because the grant is fixed and the programme is time-bound; a larger contingency would have to come out of delivery. The release rules prioritise the Filmtek risk because the nitrate window is fixed and there is no alternative nitrate scanner in the pack. The Bindwell risk has a fallback (CRO copystands and additional days).

### 9.10 Why C gets no grant spend

Spending grant on C would not produce a publishable collection, because written permission is missing and the restriction runs to 2030. It would also divert money from A and B, which are the collections that can satisfy the grant condition. A small permission-chasing effort is justified and is done in-kind; a mould treatment and scanning programme for 950 boxes is not. If the estate responds positively, C should be a separate 2026–27 project with its own budget, not a late add-on to this one.

## Appendix A — Calculations

### A.1 Collection A

- 1,800 volumes; 12% brittle = 216 volumes; plan uses the conservator's 220.
- Conservation: 220 volumes ÷ 30 working days = 7.3 volumes/day; 5 January–13 February = 30 working days.
- Scanning: 1,800 volumes ÷ 75 volumes/day = 24 scanning days; 2 February–5 March = 24 working days.
- Sensitivity: at 60 volumes/day, 1,800 ÷ 60 = 30 days; 2 February–13 March = 30 working days. Additional 6 days × £700 = £4,200.
- Throughput assumption: 75 volumes/day × about 150 exposures/volume = 11,250 exposures/day; at 1,500 exposures/hour = 7.5 hours. This is tight; validate in the first three days and adjust the daily target or add days if needed.

### A.2 Collection B

- 240 reels ÷ 24 reels/day = 10 scanning days.
- Batch: 4 reels × 6 minutes = 24 minutes scanning + 6 minutes transfer/logging = 30 minutes. Hard caps: 40 reels and 30 minutes.
- Daily: 6 batches × 4 reels = 24 reels; 6 × 30 minutes = 3 hours of batch time.
- Sensitivity: at 10 minutes/reel, 2 reels per batch (20 minutes + 10 minutes = 30), 12 batches/day = 24 reels/day, still 10 days but 6 hours/day. At 15 minutes/reel, 1 reel per batch, 24 batches/day = 12 hours/day, which is not feasible; the booking would need 20 days, beyond the contingency. This is why the day-one calibration is a hard gate.

### A.3 Collection B rights

- 240 reels × 26 minutes = 6,240 minutes = 104 hours.
- 104 hours ÷ 7 hours/day = 14.9 days; budget 15 days.

### A.4 Collection C

- 950 boxes × 8% = 76 mould-affected boxes.
- No grant spend; no scanning or treatment in 2026.

arguments.old_string: The plan spends the grant exactly within **£84,000**, including a **£5,220 contingency (6.2%)**. The critical path runs through the B rights assessment, the Filmtek booking, the A conservation work and the final publication checks. Both publication dates sit ahead of 30 June, leaving a deliberate buffer.
arguments.new_string: The plan spends the grant exactly within **£84,000**, including a **£4,620 contingency (5.5%)**. The critical path runs through the B rights assessment, the Filmtek booking, the A conservation work and the final publication checks. Both publication dates sit ahead of 30 June, leaving a deliberate buffer. The Filmtek booking is **three weeks, not the two-week minimum**, because the 30-minute nitrate window and realistic scan times allow about one reel per batch; this is the single most important calibration in the plan.

arguments.old_string:
2. **Batch size:** set on day one by a timed trial. The planning assumption is 6 minutes per reel (load, scan, unload), giving **4 reels per 30-minute batch**: 24 minutes of scanning plus 6 minutes of transfer and logging. The hard caps remain 40 reels and 30 minutes; if the trial shows a slower cycle, the batch size falls (for example, 2 reels per batch at 10 minutes per reel).
3. **Daily throughput:** at 4 reels per batch and 6 batches per day, **24 reels per day**. Ten scanning days therefore cover 240 reels, with the remaining time in each day available for QC, re-scans and cold-store returns.
4. **Cold-store discipline:** reels return to the cold store after every batch and are never left in the inspection room overnight. In/out times are logged for every batch.
5. **Environmental monitoring:** a calibrated temperature/RH logger runs throughout the booking. If the inspection room moves outside 15–20°C or 40–50% RH, scanning stops and the conservator is called.
6. **Calibration gate:** **13 February** is a calibration day, not a production run. The batch size, scan cycle time and daily throughput are recorded and approved by the conservator and Programme Manager before full scanning begins on 16 February. If the cycle time makes 240 reels unachievable in ten days, the booking is extended using contingency (see section 8) or the scope is escalated to the funder; the 30-minute rule is never relaxed.

**Throughput check:** 240 reels ÷ 24 reels/day = 10 scanning days. At 6 batches/day × 30 minutes = 3 hours of batch time per day, leaving time for handling, QC and re-scans. This fits the two-week Filmtek booking, which is the supplier's minimum.
arguments.new_string:
2. **Batch size:** the 40-reel cap is not reachable at realistic scan speeds. A professional 35mm nitrate scan is about **20–25 minutes per reel end-to-end** (loading, scanning, unloading and inspection). At 20 minutes of scanning plus 10 minutes of transfer and logging, the batch is **one reel per 30-minute window**. The hard caps remain 40 reels and 30 minutes; the 40-reel figure would only bind if the Filmtek could scan a reel in under 45 seconds, which is not assumed.
3. **Daily throughput:** at one reel per batch and 16 batches per day, **16 reels per day**. Fifteen scanning days cover 240 reels. The site day is nine hours, of which eight hours are batch time; breaks are taken between batches.
4. **Cold-store discipline:** reels return to the cold store after every batch and are never left in the inspection room overnight. In/out times are logged for every batch.
5. **Environmental monitoring:** a calibrated temperature/RH logger runs throughout the booking. If the inspection room moves outside 15–20°C or 40–50% RH, scanning stops and the conservator is called.
6. **Calibration gate:** **13 February** is a calibration day, not a production run. The batch size, scan cycle time and daily throughput are recorded and approved by the conservator and Programme Manager before full scanning begins on 16 February. If the cycle is 14 minutes or faster, two reels fit in a 30-minute batch and the booking can finish early. If it is 15–25 minutes, the one-reel batch and 15-day booking stand. If it is slower than 25 minutes, the booking is extended by up to three days from contingency (see section 8) or the scope is escalated to the funder. If a single reel cannot be scanned inside 30 minutes including handling, the conservation policy cannot be met with this scanner and the Partnership must seek a policy variation or a faster machine; the 30-minute rule is never relaxed.

**Throughput check:** 240 reels ÷ 16 reels/day = 15 scanning days. At 16 batches/day × 30 minutes = 8 hours of batch time per day. This requires a three-week Filmtek booking; the supplier's two-week minimum is not sufficient at realistic scan speeds. The third week is not padding: at 20–25 minutes per reel it is the difference between scanning all 240 reels and stopping at about 160.

arguments.old_string:
**Storage and handling.** All 240 reels remain in the Northgate cold store at 4°C and 35% RH when not being scanned. They move through the pass-through hatch into the inspection room at 16°C and 45% RH. The conservation policy's limits are applied as hard limits: no more than 40 reels out of the cold store at once, and no more than 30 minutes out of the cold store including scanning. The planning batch is 4 reels at 6 minutes/reel: 24 minutes of scanning plus 6 minutes of transfer and logging. Six batches per day give 24 reels/day; ten days give 240 reels. **13 February** is a calibration day; if the cycle is slower, the batch size is reduced (for example, 2 reels at 10 minutes/reel). A 15-minute cycle would allow only 1 reel per batch and would not fit ten days; that is an escalation trigger, not a silent fallback. Any extension is within the contingency and with the conservator's approval. The 30-minute rule is never relaxed.

**Scanning.** Filmtek is delivered and installed by 13 February and scans from 16 to 27 February. The scanner is never operated in the cold store. A calibrated temperature/RH logger runs throughout; if conditions leave 15–20°C or 40–50% RH, scanning stops. Each evening, files are copied to an encrypted drive and carried to CRO; the drive is logged, virus-checked, checksum-verified and ingested. No B files are left only at Northgate.

**QC and publication.** B QC and metadata run from 2 to 20 March. Every reel is checked for image integrity, frame count, colour, stability and file naming; the rights record is linked to the catalogue record. B publishes on 15 April, leaving ten weeks before the grant deadline.

At a realistic 20–25 minutes per reel end-to-end, the planning batch is **one reel per 30-minute window**, not four. Sixteen batches per day give **16 reels/day**; fifteen days give 240 reels. **13 February** is a calibration day. If it is slower than 25 minutes, the booking is extended by up to three days from contingency or escalated; if a single reel cannot be completed inside 30 minutes, the policy cannot be met with this scanner. The 30-minute rule is never relaxed.

arguments.old_string:
### 9.4 Why the Filmtek booking is exactly two weeks

Filmtek requires a two-week booking; ten working days is the minimum purchase. At the planning rate of 24 reels/day, ten days cover 240 reels with time each day for QC, re-scans and cold-store returns. A longer booking would add £1,200/day and is not needed on the planning assumptions. The 13 February calibration is the control: if the cycle is slower, the batch size falls and the booking is extended only if the contingency can cover it.
arguments.new_string:
### 9.4 Why the Filmtek booking is three weeks, not the two-week minimum

The conservation policy, not the supplier, sets the throughput. Nitrate may leave the cold store for at most 30 minutes including scanning. A realistic professional 35mm nitrate scan is 20–25 minutes per reel end-to-end; adding transfer and logging, one reel fills the 30-minute window. That gives 16 reels/day at 16 batches/day and **15 scanning days for 240 reels**. A two-week booking would stop at about 160 reels, leaving 80 unscanned and the two-collection condition unmet. The three-week booking costs an extra £6,000, which is funded by reducing management, QC and metadata days and publication polish, not by cutting conservation, scanning or rights work. If the 13 February calibration shows a 14-minute or faster cycle, two reels fit per batch and the third week is released or used for QC and re-scans; it is insurance, not padding.

arguments.old_string:
### 9.9 Why the budget has a 6.2% contingency

The two throughput assumptions — 75 volumes/day on Bindwell and 24 reels/day on Filmtek — are planning assumptions, not contractual guarantees. A 6.2% contingency covers a modest overrun on either, not both at full extent. It is deliberately not larger because the grant is fixed and the programme is time-bound; a larger contingency would have to come out of delivery. The release rules prioritise the Filmtek risk because the nitrate window is fixed and there is no alternative nitrate scanner in the pack. The Bindwell risk has a fallback (CRO copystands, additional days and limited virement from publication polish).

### A.2 Collection B

- 240 reels ÷ 24 reels/day = 10 scanning days.
- Batch: 4 reels × 6 minutes = 24 minutes scanning + 6 minutes transfer/logging = 30 minutes. Hard caps: 40 reels and 30 minutes.
- Daily: 6 batches × 4 reels = 24 reels; 6 × 30 minutes = 3 hours of batch time.
- Sensitivity: at 10 minutes/reel, 2 reels per batch (20 minutes + 10 minutes = 30), 12 batches/day = 24 reels/day, still 10 days but 6 hours/day. At 15 minutes/reel, 1 reel per batch, 24 batches/day = 12 hours/day, which is not feasible; the booking would need 20 days, beyond the contingency. This is why the 13 February calibration is a hard gate.
arguments.new_string:
### A.2 Collection B

- 240 reels ÷ 16 reels/day = 15 scanning days.
- Batch: 1 reel per 30-minute window; 20–25 minutes scanning plus 5–10 minutes transfer/logging = 25–30 minutes. Hard caps: 40 reels and 30 minutes. The 40-reel cap does not bind at realistic scan speeds.
- Daily: 16 batches × 1 reel = 16 reels; 16 × 30 minutes = 8 hours of batch time in a nine-hour site day.
- Sensitivity: at 14 minutes/reel, 2 reels per batch (28 minutes + 2 minutes handling = 30), 16 batches/day = 32 reels/day, and the booking can finish in 7.5 days. At 25 minutes/reel, 1 reel + 5 minutes = 30, 16 reels/day, 15 days. At 30 minutes/reel, there is no handling margin; 14 batches/day = 14 reels, 17.1 days, so three extra days are needed and the contingency is used. Above 30 minutes/reel, a single reel cannot be completed inside the policy window; the Partnership must seek a policy variation or a faster scanner. This is why the 13 February calibration is a hard gate.
